title: Lewis Bonding, Electron Pairs and the Octet Rule

pages.title: Why do atoms stay together?

blocks.text: Hydrogen and oxygen combine into water with properties unlike either element. A chemical bond is an interaction that holds atoms or ions together in a stable chemical species.
The key physical question is energy: the bonded arrangement must be favourable compared with the separated pieces. Lewis ideas track valence electrons to explain many common bonding patterns.

pages.transition: Track the outer electrons before proposing a bonding arrangement.

pages.title: Draw the electrons that participate

blocks.text: A Lewis symbol places dots around an element symbol to represent valence electrons. Sodium has one dot; magnesium two; chlorine seven. Inner electrons and nucleus form the kernel and are not drawn individually.
These dots are bookkeeping symbols, not photographs of electron locations. Their number connects a main-group element’s outer configuration with its common combining capacity.

Place single valence dots around separate sides of a symbol before pairing, as a bookkeeping convention. A chlorine symbol has seven dots: three pairs and one single. The unpaired dot suggests a simple opportunity to share one pair with another atom.

pages.transition: One option is to form oppositely charged ions through transfer.

pages.title: Explain electron transfer with charge balance

blocks.text: Sodium can lose one electron to form Na⁺ with a neon-like configuration; chlorine can gain one to form Cl⁻ with an argon-like configuration. Oppositely charged ions attract in the ionic solid.
For calcium fluoride, Ca²⁺ needs two F⁻ ions for neutrality, giving CaF₂. Electron transfer explains ion formation; the stabilising interactions throughout the solid complete the bonding picture.

pages.transition: Atoms can also stabilise a molecule by sharing pairs.

pages.title: Share a pair instead of transferring it

blocks.text: In H₂, two H atoms share one electron pair. Each counts that pair towards a stable two-electron shell, a duplet. A shared pair represents one covalent bond, drawn as a line.
Cl₂ shares one pair while each Cl retains three lone pairs. A lone pair belongs to one atom in the Lewis representation; a bonding pair is counted around both bonded atoms.

pages.transition: More than one shared pair gives multiple-bond possibilities.

pages.title: Build double and triple bonds

blocks.text: O₂ is represented with a double bond: two shared pairs. N₂ has a triple bond: three shared pairs. Sharing can therefore complete octets without assuming all bonding involves full electron transfer.
The octet rule describes a common tendency towards eight valence electrons around an atom. Hydrogen seeks a duplet. The rule is a useful pattern, not the fundamental cause of every bond.

pages.transition: Use the full electron total to build an explicit structure.

pages.title: Construct a Lewis structure step by step

blocks.text: For CO₂, total valence electrons=4+2×6=16. Connect O–C–O using four electrons. Complete terminal O octets, then move one lone pair from each O into bonding pairs to complete carbon’s octet.
The result O=C=O uses sixteen electrons: eight in bonds and eight in oxygen lone pairs. Each atom has an octet. Check both total electron count and each atom’s surrounding count.

pages.transition: Formal charge provides another check on the resulting drawing.

pages.title: Calculate formal charge

blocks.text: Formal charge=valence electrons−non-bonding electrons−half the bonding electrons. It assigns the bonding electrons equally, making it a bookkeeping charge rather than a measured partial charge.
For NH₄⁺, N contributes five valence electrons, has zero non-bonding electrons and eight bonding electrons: FC(N)=5−0−4=+1. Each H has 1−0−1=0; the sum is+1.

Check formal charge in CO₂ drawn O=C=O. Carbon has 4−0−8/2=0. Each oxygen has 6−4−4/2=0. The zero sum matches the neutral molecule; the calculation does not assert equal physical sharing in each polar C–O bond.

pages.transition: Electron accounting must still work when octets are incomplete or exceeded.

pages.title: Identify exceptions rather than force octets

blocks.text: BF₃ has only six electrons around B in its simple Lewis structure. NO has an odd total electron count, preventing all atoms from having paired octets. Expanded-octet Lewis representations occur for species such as PF₅ and SF₆.

Never invent extra electrons to force every species into an octet. The structure must retain the actual electron total and ionic charge. Second-period atoms do not expand their valence shell in this elementary treatment.

pages.transition: A useful electron diagram has limits that require further bonding models.

pages.title: Know what Lewis diagrams cannot predict

blocks.text: Lewis structures help track connectivity, electron pairs and formal charges. They do not by themselves predict accurate three-dimensional shapes, bond strengths or every magnetic property.

Clarification: expanded-octet drawings are useful bookkeeping. Modern bonding does not require literal occupation of low-energy valence d hybrids to explain every hypervalent main-group molecule; later textbook hybridisation labels are models, not direct measurements.

pages.transition: Review the construction checks without forcing every species into an octet.

pages.title: Check electrons before accepting a structure

blocks.text: Count all valence electrons, add electrons for a negative charge or subtract for a positive charge, form bonds, complete appropriate shells and check formal charges. The formal charges must sum to the species charge.

Octets and duplets guide many simple examples, but incomplete, odd-electron and expanded-octet cases show their limits. A valid drawing needs correct electron accounting before further shape predictions.

questions.question: Why are only valence electrons shown as Lewis dots?
questions.answer: They are the electrons mainly involved in the elementary bonding description; inner electrons are included in the kernel.

questions.question: Why is CaF₂ the neutral formula?
questions.answer: One Ca²⁺ balances two F⁻ ions.

questions.question: How many valence electrons are available for CO₂?
Calculate nitrogen’s formal charge in NH₄⁺.
questions.answer: 5−0−8/2=+1; all hydrogens have formal charge zero.

questions.question: Does formal charge equal an atom’s actual charge distribution?
questions.answer: No. It assumes equal sharing of bonding electrons and is a bookkeeping quantity.

questions.question: Why does NO not satisfy paired octets for both atoms?
questions.answer: Its odd total number of valence electrons cannot be divided entirely into pairs.

questions.question: Can Lewis structure alone establish molecular shape?
questions.answer: No. A three-dimensional model such as VSEPR is needed.
